ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in $\triangle ABC$, $AC=BC$, circle O is the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, and the extension of $BO$ intersects side $AC$ at point D. When $\triangle ABD$ is an isosceles triangle, what is the measure of $\angle A$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Connect OC, \\
$\because$ $CA=CB$, \\
$\therefore$ $\overset{\frown}{CA}=\overset{\frown}{CB}$, $\angle CAB=\angle CBA$, \\
$\therefore$ $OC\perp AB$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle DCO=\angle BCO$, \\
$\because$ $OC=OB$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle OBC=\angle BCO$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle ADB=3\angle OBC$, \\
When $BA=BD$, $\angle A=\angle BDA=3\angle OBC$, \\
Then $8\angle OBC=180^\circ$, \\
Solving for: $\angle OBC=22.5^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle A=67.5^\circ$; \\
When $AB=AD$, $\angle ABD=\angle BDA=3\angle OBC$, \\
Then $10\angle OBC=180^\circ$, \\
Solving for: $\angle OBC=18^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle A=\angle ABD+\angle OBC=4\angle OBC=72^\circ$, \\
The case for DA=DB does not exist, \\
In summary, when $\triangle ABD$ is an isosceles triangle, the degree of $\angle A$ is $67.5^\circ$ or $72^\circ$, \\
Hence the answer is: $\boxed{67.5^\circ}$ or $\boxed{72^\circ}$.

method.method_draft: Use an analytic-coordinate setup based on the diagram. Put the circumcircle as the unit circle with O=(0,0), take the symmetry axis OC vertical as shown, set C=(0,1), and let α=∠A. Because AC=BC, A and B are symmetric about OC, and since ∠A subtends arc BC, the central angle ∠BOC=2α. Thus choose B=(sin2α,cos2α) and A=(−sin2α,cos2α). The displayed configuration has D on side AC and on the extension of BO beyond O, so write D=−λB with λ>0. Intersect D=−λB with the line AC; solving A+s(C−A)=−λB gives λ=1/(1−2cos2α) and s=1−λ. Then compute the three side lengths of triangle ABD: AB=2sin2α, BD=1+λ, and AD=2sinα(1−λ). raw_record.original_question: In $\triangle ABC$, $AC=BC$, circle $O$ is the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, and the extension of $BO$ intersects side $AC$ at point $D$. When $\triangle ABD$ is an isosceles triangle, what is the measure of $\angle A$?
raw_record.answer: Solution: Connect $OC$. Because $CA=CB$, therefore $\overset{\frown}{CA}=\overset{\frown}{CB}$ and $\angle CAB=\angle CBA$. Therefore $OC\perp AB$. Therefore $\angle DCO=\angle BCO$. Because $OC=OB$, therefore $\angle OBC=\angle BCO$. Therefore $\angle ADB=3\angle OBC$. When $BA=BD$, $\angle A=\angle BDA=3\angle OBC$. Then $8\angle OBC=180^\circ$, so $\angle OBC=22.5^\circ$, and thus $\angle A=67.5^\circ$. When $AB=AD$, $\angle ABD=\angle BDA=3\angle OBC$. Then $10\angle OBC=180^\circ$, so $\angle OBC=18^\circ$, and thus $\angle A=\angle ABD+\angle OBC=4\angle OBC=72^\circ$. The case $DA=DB$ does not exist. In summary, when $\triangle ABD$ is an isosceles triangle, $\angle A$ is $67.5^\circ$ or $72^\circ$. Hence the answer is $\boxed{67.5^\circ}$ or $\boxed{72^\circ}$.
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, there is triangle ABC inside a circle, A is at the lower left of the circle, B is at the lower right of the circle, and C is at the top of the circle; O is marked inside the circle near the lower middle position and is the center of the circle; D is located on side AC; the straight line starting from B and passing through O continues to extend to D, so B, O, D are collinear. Reasoning: Connect OC. Let x=∠OBC. Because AC=BC, triangle ABC is an isosceles triangle, and ∠A=∠B. Also because the distances from C to A and B are equal, C lies on the perpendicular bisector of chord AB; O is the center of the circle and also lies on the perpendicular bisector of chord AB, so OC⊥AB. Because OB=OC, triangle OBC is an isosceles triangle, ∠BCO=x, hence ∠BOC=180°−2x. From OC⊥AB, ∠ABC=90°−x can be obtained. Also ∠ABC=∠ABO+∠OBC, so ∠ABO=90°−2x. Since D is on line BO, ∠ABD=90°−2x; also AD is on AC, so ∠BAD=∠A=90°−x. Therefore in triangle ABD, ∠ADB=180°−(90°−x)−(90°−2x)=3x. Now check the three cases in which triangle ABD is an isosceles triangle: If BA=BD, then the base angles ∠BAD=∠ADB, so 90°−x=3x, giving x=22.5°, therefore ∠A=90°−x=67.5°. If AB=AD, then the base angles ∠ABD=∠ADB, so 90°−2x=3x, giving x=18°, therefore ∠A=90°−x=72°. If AD=BD, then the base angles ∠BAD=∠ABD, so 90°−x=90°−2x, giving x=0, which does not accord with a non-degenerate figure, so it does not exist. In summary, the possible values of ∠A are 67.5° or 72°.
